generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, the goals you set shape how much you get from a module. A performance goal fixes on one mark, such as a grade for a single assignment. A mastery goal aims at a capability you will reuse across the whole degree, such as building an argument or weighing evidence. Turning a vague aim into a mastery goal is what keeps your learning moving forward.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students who set themselves a goal at the start of a new module.

Student A writes down a single aim: get at least 65 in the final assignment. It is specific, but it is a performance goal fixed on one mark. When an early task does not count towards that assignment, Student A puts little into it, and the goal gives no guidance on how to actually improve.

Student B starts with the same vague wish to do well, but rephrases it: get better at weighing the evidence behind a claim. That is a mastery goal, aimed at a capability rather than one mark. It guides every task on the module, counting or not, because each one is a chance to practise the skill the goal names.

Both students set a goal. Only Student B's goal moved their learning forward across the whole module.
generatedProse.summary: Goals come in two kinds: performance goals target a mark, while mastery goals build a capability that lasts beyond one task. A vague aim is neither until you make it specific. You can now tell the two apart, rephrase a loose aim into a mastery goal, and set one of your own. With mindset, motivation and goals all working, you are ready to keep progressing.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Student B's goal move their learning forward where Student A's did not?

items.text: It aimed at a reusable capability, so it guided every task on the module.
It set a higher target mark than Student A's goal.
It was written down more neatly.
It focused only on the final assignment that counted.

feedback.correct: That's right. The mastery goal aimed at a capability, so it guided every task, counting or not.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what let Student B's goal guide work across the whole module.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Student B's goal moved learning forward because it aimed at a reusable capability and guided every task. The others stay fixed on a single mark.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
